Executive Summary

Live digital sports broadcasting represents one of the most volatile and unforgiving traffic profiles in modern cloud computing. Unlike global video-on-demand platforms (e.g., Netflix) where traffic is temporally dispersed across multiple time zones, live cricket streaming in India concentrates tens of millions of concurrent connections on the same origin infrastructure at the exact same second. Driven by real-time mobile push notifications, match start times, boundaries, and wickets, user traffic arrives not as a smooth, predictable curve, but as an abrupt "traffic tsunami". Over eight years of rapid platform scaling, Hotstar's peak concurrent viewership expanded more than thirteen-fold—from 4.7 million in 2017 to an unprecedented, company-reported 61.2 million concurrent viewers during the 2025 ICC Champions Trophy final.

Primary engineering disclosures from Hotstar and AWS reveal that conventional reactive autoscaling—relying on CloudWatch alarms to detect CPU saturation and launch virtual machines—consistently failed during live cricket matches. Physical provisioning overheads (virtual machine allocation, operating system bootstrap, container image pulling, application worker initialization, and load balancer health checks) create an unavoidable scale-out lag of 2 to 4 minutes. In cricket, 6 to 8 million viewers arrive in under 120 seconds. Consequently, unserved incoming traffic saturates existing compute instances, causing thread pool starvation, multi-second latency spikes, HTTP 504 gateway timeouts, and aggressive client retries that trigger cascading backend failure before reactive instances can become healthy.

Hotstar resolved this bottleneck through an evolving multi-tier architecture: 1. Pre-Scaling with Concurrency Ladders (2018): Bypassing reactive scaling by pre-provisioning fixed EC2 instance capacity 30 to 60 minutes ahead of matches using predictive viewership models. 2. Containerization & Custom Autoscalers (2019): Migrating core services to Docker on self-managed Kubernetes clusters, slashing boot times and reducing compute waste tenfold. 3. Datacenter Abstraction & Envoy Gateway Mesh (2023–2025): Eliminating an architectural bottleneck of 200+ external Application Load Balancers and cross-cluster "hairpinning" by deploying an Envoy-based internal API gateway, migrating to managed Amazon EKS across 6 clusters in ap-south-1, implementing sub-minute node scaling with Karpenter, and adopting graceful feature shedding ("Jettison") to guarantee 100% compute allocation to live video delivery.

Following Theme 1 of the IT457 curriculum, Group 19 designed, deployed, and empirically evaluated an end-to-end Cloud Proof of Concept (PoC) on Amazon Web Services (AWS) in region ap-south-1 (Mumbai). The PoC implements a stateless Python FastAPI service deployed on t3.micro EC2 instances distributed across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and managed by an Auto Scaling Group (ASG). The cluster is governed by an explicit CloudWatch alarm: when average CPU utilization exceeds 50%, add another instance.

Using Locust, we subjected the live infrastructure to a 13-minute event-shaped traffic spike executing 55,910 live HTTP requests. As load surged from 20 to 150 concurrent viewers, CPU crossed the 50% threshold, triggering CloudWatch alarm actions that dynamically scaled the group from 1 to 4 instances. Under 4 healthy instances, median response time plummeted from 590 ms to 73 ms, and p95 latency dropped from 2,100 ms to 330 ms—representing an 84% reduction in tail latency with an overall 99.58% request success rate. Following traffic termination, the CloudWatch low-CPU alarm (< 20%) triggered automated scale-in, verified through ALB connection draining. The entire experiment ran within AWS Free Tier limits at $0.00 total expenditure.

1. Introduction & Research Objectives

1.1 Context & Problem Statement

In high-concurrency digital broadcasting, video delivery reliability is paramount. Streaming platforms like Hotstar (now JioHotstar) serve a massive mobile-first user base across India. When a high-stakes cricket match begins, millions of viewers launch the application simultaneously. If origin APIs fail to respond, mobile clients retry aggressively with exponential backoff disabled, turning temporary spikes into total system collapse.

2. Case Study: Hotstar’s Architectural Evolution

Hotstar’s cloud infrastructure underwent three major architectural revolutions to handle the scaling demands of live cricket streaming.

Figure 1: Hotstar High-Level Production Architecture (ByteByteGo Reference). Ingress traffic passes from heterogeneous client devices through an external CDN gateway and VPC ALBs into an internal Envoy gateway, routing to microservices on Amazon EKS and backend managed datastores.

2.1 The "Tsunami" Problem & Scale-Out Lag

Hotstar defines its traffic profile as a tsunami, characterized by three structural challenges: * Match-Start Shock: 6–8 million viewers launch the application within two minutes of the first ball. Watch-page and homepage API traffic surges by 300% to 500%. * The Mathematics of Scale-Out Lag: In the 2019 World Cup, concurrency expanded at a rate exceeding 1,000,000 viewers per minute. Standard EC2 virtual machine boot, package initialization, and target health checking take 2 to 3 minutes. In simple arithmetic: $$\text{Unserved Demand} = 1{,}000{,}000 \text{ viewers/min} \times 2.5 \text{ min} = 2{,}500{,}000 \text{ viewers}$$ Over 2.5 million users arrive before a single additional VM can accept traffic. If an infrastructure relies solely on reactive scaling, existing servers become CPU-saturated, queues overflow, requests time out with HTTP 504 errors, and client retries trigger a self-inflicted Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS). * Cascading Failures: When origin APIs fail to respond, mobile clients retry aggressively with exponential backoff disabled, turning temporary spikes into total system collapse.

2.2 Evolution Across Three Architectural Eras

Era 1 (2018): Monolithic EC2 and Static "Ladders"

  • Infrastructure: Services deployed directly on bare EC2 virtual machines behind 200+ AWS Classic Load Balancers.
  • Scaling Strategy: Reactive autoscaling was discarded. Instead, capacity was sized ahead of matches using concurrency ladders: pre-provisioning fixed tiers of EC2 instances 30 to 60 minutes before scheduled match times based on historical models.
  • Drawbacks: Massive financial waste during uncompetitive matches; inability to react if an ordinary match became unexpectedly thrilling; regional AWS EC2 provisioning rate-limits (RequestLimitExceeded).

Era 2 (2019): Containerization, Self-Managed Kubernetes, and the Hairpinning Crisis

  • Infrastructure: Migration to Docker containers running on two large self-managed Kubernetes clusters on EC2.
  • Scaling Strategy: Developed a proprietary custom autoscaler that evaluated traffic velocity (rate of change) in addition to CPU. The algorithm was run in "shadow mode" for months before driving production capacity.
  • Impact: Delivered 25.3M peak concurrency with roughly 10x less compute capacity by packing containers tightly onto EC2 Spot instances.

Figure 2: The Service-to-Service Hairpinning Bottleneck in Era 2 (ByteByteGo Reference). Internal microservice communication traversed Route 53 and public/external ALBs, creating latency amplification, port exhaustion, and operational fragility.

In-Depth Breakdown: The Hairpinning Bottleneck

As illustrated in Figure 2, Era 2 introduced severe systemic friction in service-to-service communication: 1. The ALB Hairpin Loop: When Service B (e.g., Watch Session service) in Kubernetes Cluster 1 needed to call Service A (e.g., User Entitlement or Catalog service) in Cluster 2 (or even within the same cluster), it did not communicate over an internal pod network. Instead, Service B made an outbound HTTP call to service-a.hotstar.com. This resolved via Amazon Route 53 to an external Application Load Balancer sitting outside the cluster! The request exited the node, traversed AWS networking to the ALB, and hairpinned back into the cluster to reach Service A. 2. 200+ Load Balancers & Pre-Warming Tickets: Every single microservice had its own dedicated ALB. AWS ALBs scale by adding IP addresses behind DNS, which takes time. For sudden cricket surges, 200+ ALBs could not scale fast enough. Hotstar engineers had to manually open high-severity AWS Support tickets days before every tournament to request manual ALB pre-warming for over 200 load balancers. 3. NodePort Range Exhaustion: Target Groups routed traffic to Kubernetes worker nodes using NodePort. The Kubernetes NodePort range is strictly limited to ports 30000–32767 (only 2,767 usable ports across the entire cluster). As services multiplied, port collisions and exhaustion became critical failure modes. 4. VPC IP Exhaustion & Kube-API Overload: Rapid pod scale-out saturated AWS VPC /24 subnet CIDR allocations. Simultaneously, running hundreds of services on two monolithic clusters overwhelmed the Kubernetes control plane (kube-apiserver and etcd raft consensus locks).

Era 3 (2023–2025): Datacenter Abstraction and Envoy Mesh

To eliminate the hairpinning crisis, solve IP exhaustion, and prepare for 50M+ concurrent viewers under the "Free on Mobile" initiative, Hotstar completely overhauled its cloud architecture.

Figure 3: Modern Datacenter Abstraction Architecture (ByteByteGo Reference). Ingress ALBs forward traffic to a centralized Envoy API Gateway mesh. Microservices communicate internally within the VPC boundary, eliminating 200+ ALBs and external hairpinning.

Core Architectural Innovations in Era 3

  1. Datacenter Abstraction: Hotstar grouped multiple managed Amazon EKS clusters within an AWS region into a single logical "Datacenter". Development teams are granted a unified namespace per datacenter and deploy to designated clusters, while platform-level routing abstracts underlying cluster boundaries.
  2. Elimination of ALB Hairpinning via Envoy Mesh: As shown in Figure 3, the 200+ legacy per-service load balancers were replaced by an Envoy-based internal API gateway mesh. Incoming public requests pass from Route 53 through consolidated ingress ALBs directly to Envoy. Crucially, all service-to-service calls remain entirely within the internal VPC network boundary via Envoy service discovery. No traffic hairpins out to external load balancers, completely eliminating the need for AWS ALB pre-warming tickets.
  3. Cluster Isolation & Modern Networking:
  4. Workloads are partitioned across six managed Amazon EKS clusters (running Kubernetes 1.24+). High-priority Tier-1 services run in isolated clusters to limit blast radiuses.
  5. Migrated from NodePort to ClusterIP backed by the AWS VPC CNI. Subnets were expanded from /24 to massive /19 CIDR blocks (8,190 IP addresses per subnet), eliminating IP exhaustion.
  6. Per-Subnet NAT Gateways: NAT Gateways were deployed per-subnet rather than per-AZ, preventing inter-AZ data transfer bottlenecks and cross-zone charges.
  7. Sub-Minute Node Elasticity with Karpenter: Migrated from the legacy Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler to Karpenter. Karpenter bypasses ASG node group abstractions, directly querying EC2 fleet APIs to provision right-sized compute nodes (using flexible Spot instance pools) in under 45 seconds.
  8. Edge Shielding & Graceful Degradation ("Jettison"):
  9. Edge CDN Offload: Akamai and AWS CloudFront terminate TLS at the edge, serving 95%+ of video chunk requests (.m4s/HLS manifests) directly from cache. Only dynamic, non-cacheable APIs reach the origin EKS clusters.
  10. Controlled Degradation ("Jettison"): When origin compute crosses saturation thresholds, Hotstar’s Envoy gateway programmatically sheds non-essential Tier-2/Tier-3 features (user comments, live emoji reactions, interactive polls, real-time match stats, personalized recommendation carousels). This guarantees that 100% of origin compute and bandwidth remain dedicated to stream entitlement and playlist generation.

3. Cloud Proof of Concept (PoC) Architecture

To evaluate the core mechanism of cloud elasticity without incurring enterprise costs, Group 19 built a focused Cloud Proof of Concept matching Theme 1 of the course rubric.

Figure 4: IT457 Group 19 Cloud Proof of Concept Architecture. A high-concurrency Locust swarm targets an AWS Application Load Balancer in ap-south-1, distributing traffic across a multi-AZ Auto Scaling Group governed by CloudWatch 50% CPU alarms.

3.1 Application Microservice (app.py)

Implemented in Python 3.12 using FastAPI and served by Uvicorn with 2 worker processes (matching the 2 vCPUs on a t3.micro): * GET /: Returns {"status": "Stream available", "service": "hotstar-cloud-scaling-poc", "instance": INSTANCE_ID}. Returning the EC2 instance ID confirms traffic distribution across dynamic servers. * GET /health: Health-check endpoint returning HTTP 200 {"ok": true, "status": "healthy"} for ALB Target Group polling every 15 seconds. * GET /work?n=300000: Executes CPU-intensive arithmetic ($n=300,000$ iterations), consuming ~25–40 ms of CPU per request. Under concurrent load, this saturates vCPU cores to push utilization past 50%.

3.2 Infrastructure-as-Code (hotstar-fastapi-cfn.yaml)

The entire infrastructure was provisioned via a 1-click AWS CloudFormation template: * Networking: 2-Availability-Zone VPC (10.50.0.0/16) in ap-south-1 (Mumbai) with public subnets and Internet Gateway. * Security: ALB accepts public HTTP 80; EC2 instances accept TCP 8000 exclusively from the ALB security group. * Launch Template: Amazon Linux 2023 on Free Tier t3.micro (2 vCPUs, 1 GB RAM). EC2 UserData installs Python, writes app.py, and starts a systemd service (hotstar-poc.service). Detailed 1-minute CloudWatch monitoring enabled. * Auto Scaling Group (hotstar-asg): Min: 1, Desired: 1, Max: 4. Health check type: ELB (grace period: 120s). * Course 50% CPU Rule Implementation: - Scale-Out: CloudWatch Alarm hotstar-cpu-high-scale-out triggers when average ASG CPU > 50% for two consecutive 60s periods $\rightarrow$ executes ScaleOutPolicy (+1 instance, cooldown 120s). - Scale-In: CloudWatch Alarm hotstar-cpu-low-scale-in triggers when average ASG CPU < 20% for ten consecutive 60s periods $\rightarrow$ executes ScaleInPolicy (-1 instance, cooldown 300s).

4. Experimental Methodology

4.1 Match-Shaped Traffic Profile

Using Locust (loadtest/locustfile.py), we executed a realistic 13-minute event profile: * Phase 1 (0–120s): 20 users (steady match buildup baseline). * Phase 2 (120–180s): Rapid ramp to 150 users (the match-start traffic tsunami). * Phase 3 (180–600s): 150 sustained concurrent users (holds heavy load to trigger ASG scale-out). * Phase 4 (600–720s): Rapid drop back to 20 users (match conclusion). * Phase 5 (720–780s): Tail recovery baseline (observing automated scale-in).

4.2 Telemetry & Polling

  • Locust Client Metrics: Recorded timestamps, response times, percentile distributions, and failure codes every second to results/raw/locust_stats_history.csv.
  • ASG Instance Tracking: Our dual-mode poller (loadtest/poller.py) sampled in-service instance counts every 10 seconds, logging to results/raw/instances.csv.
  • Cloud Telemetry Alignment: Data was synchronized using analysis/plot.py, matching Locust latency windows with corresponding AWS in-service instance counts via pd.merge_asof.

5.3 Key Architectural Observations

  1. Quantification of Scale-Out Lag:
    When the 150-user tsunami hit at $t = 120\text{s}$, the single instance saturated instantly, pushing CPU past 50%. The CloudWatch alarm required 2 evaluation periods (120s) to transition to In alarm. An additional ~60 seconds elapsed for EC2 boot, Python dependency verification, and ALB health check passing. During this ~180-second window, p95 latency peaked at 2,100 ms, and 234 requests timed out. This reproduces the exact historical problem Hotstar experienced in 2018.
  2. Cluster Stabilization at 4 Instances:
    Once the ASG scaled to its configured maximum of 4 instances, the Application Load Balancer distributed the 150 concurrent users evenly (~37 concurrent requests per VM). CPU per instance stabilized below 45%, and median p50 latency dropped to 73 ms.
  3. Scale-In and Connection Draining:
    When Locust stopped traffic at $t = 780\text{s}$, CPU utilization dropped to ~0%. CloudWatch alarm hotstar-cpu-low-scale-in detected CPU < 20% and initiated scale-in. In the Target Group dashboard, instances transitioned to Draining state, allowing existing TCP connections to close cleanly before terminating the virtual machines.

7.2 Scaled Cost Modeling (Hotstar Scale Comparison)

To understand commercial cloud economics, we model Hotstar's origin tier during a 3-hour cricket match: * Hotstar peak requires ~2,000 compute nodes (e.g., c5.2xlarge with 8 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM at $0.34/hr in Mumbai). * Pure Over-Provisioning (Era 1): Running 2,000 instances statically for 8 hours = $5,440 per match day. * Auto-Scaling with Spot Instances (Era 2 & 3): Scaling dynamically from 200 to 2,000 nodes using 70% Spot instances ($0.10/hr) cuts origin compute cost to approximately $680 per match day—an 87.5% compute cost reduction.

8. Discussion, Limitations & Lessons Learned

8.1 Why Not a Master-Slave Database or Redis Cache?

In production systems design, stateful data is separated from stateless delivery: 1. Stateless Origin Model: Video chunks (.m4s/HLS) are static assets cached at the edge CDN (95%+ hit ratio). If 60 million viewers hit a relational database on every ball, the database connection pool would instantly deadlock. 2. Isolation of Variables: Per the course rubric, Theme 1 evaluates compute elasticity. Adding a database would introduce connection-pool bottlenecks, masking the Auto Scaling Group's CPU response.

8.2 Limitations of the Proof of Concept

  • Scale Difference: The PoC models core infrastructure dynamics using 150 concurrent users across 4 instances, whereas Hotstar scales across 6 EKS clusters handling 61.2 million concurrent streams.
  • Origin-Only Scope: The PoC does not include an edge CDN tier, DRM encryption keys, or multi-bitrate video transcoding.

10. Viva Defense: Essential Questions & Answers

  1. Q: Why was 50% CPU chosen as the threshold instead of 80% or 90%?
    A: Booting a new EC2 instance, running user data, and passing ALB health checks takes 2 to 3 minutes (scale-out lag). Setting the threshold at 50% provides safety headroom so existing instances do not crash from queue saturation while new capacity is booting.
  2. Q: Why did p95 latency spike to 2,100 ms at 2 instances before dropping to 330 ms at 4 instances?
    A: This directly demonstrates scale-out lag. When the 150-user traffic surge hit, the initial instance was saturated before instance #2 became in-service and healthy. Once instances #3 and #4 joined the pool, request concurrency was distributed, slashing latency by 84%.
  3. Q: Why did Hotstar move from reactive autoscaling to pre-scaling ladders?
    A: Because live cricket traffic surges arrive in under 90 seconds. Cloud VM provisioning takes minutes; reactive autoscaling always lags behind match-start bursts. Hotstar pre-provisions capacity in advance based on predicted viewership curves.
  4. Q: What was the service hairpinning problem in Hotstar's Era 2, and how did Envoy solve it in Era 3?
    A: In Era 2, internal microservices called each other through Route 53 and external ALBs. This hairpinned traffic through external networks, required 200+ ALBs to be manually pre-warmed before every tournament, and exhausted NodePort ranges (30000-32767). In Era 3, Hotstar adopted a Datacenter Abstraction with an Envoy API Gateway mesh. Service calls stay within the VPC network, eliminating 200+ ALBs and eliminating hairpinning completely.
  5. Q: What is the purpose of connection draining?
    A: Connection draining (deregistration delay) instructs the ALB to stop routing new requests to an instance being scaled in, allowing existing in-flight HTTP requests to complete cleanly before the VM is terminated.
